title: A high-speed, large-aperture 3D printed laser shutter for cold atom experiments
authors: Samantha L. Rubinstein, Charles W. Woffinden, Maarten T. M. Christenhusz, Guillaume Gauthier, Tyler W. Neely
abstract: Cold atom experiments require optical shutters with rapid and repeatable actuation. Existing solutions often involve high cost, limited aperture diameter and slow transitioning. We present a 3D-printable shutter design featuring a large aperture of 4.5 mm diameter, low-cost assembly, and robust performance. The device achieves switching times of $399\pm8~μ$s with delays of $2.7\pm0.2$ ms for a fully illuminated aperture, with four different shutters demonstrating repeatable performance. We measure the shutter speed to be $7.0\pm0.1$ m/s. This approach offers an accessible, scalable solution for cold atom and other optical experiments requiring multiple shutters with precise light control and avoids the need to resize or precision-align a beam through an aperture.
summary: This paper presents a novel, high-speed, and large-aperture laser shutter fabricated using 3D printing for use in cold atom experiments. The device achieves fast switching times and high repeatability, overcoming limitations of existing, expensive, or small-aperture commercial shutters. It provides an accessible and scalable solution for precise light control in quantum physics setups.
main_problem: Cold atom experiments require optical shutters that are rapid, repeatable, and have a large aperture, as existing solutions are often costly, small, or slow.
main_result: The authors developed a 3D-printable laser shutter achieving a large 4.5 mm aperture with fast switching times ($399 \mu	ext{s}$) and high repeatability, offering an accessible alternative for optical control.
method: The system was built using 3D printing and driven by an H-bridge circuit, with performance characterized by measuring delay and transition times using a fast photodiode.
model_or_system: The physical system is a custom, 3D-printed laser shutter designed for cold atom applications. It uses a mechanical blade actuated by an electronic circuit to precisely control the passage of a laser beam.
key_observables: Switching times ($399 \mu	ext{s}$), delay times ($2.7 	ext{ ms}$), shutter speed ($7.0 	ext{ ms}^{-1}$), and optical power handling capacity ($>100 	ext{ mW}$).
important_parameters: Aperture diameter ($4.5 	ext{ mm}$), operating voltage ($	ext{VCC}$ range), and the need to minimize bounce and optical leakage.
main_assumptions: The design assumes the use of 3D printing materials (PLA+, Onyx) and that the electronic control (RC network) can reliably drive the motor for high speed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the delay time and bounce parameters via photodiode response, show the CAD design, and plot performance metrics (transition/delay times) against the applied supply voltage ($	ext{VCC}$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of optical control in cold atom experiments, details the novel 3D-printed mechanical and electronic design, presents comprehensive characterization data (speed, repeatability, stability), and concludes by positioning the device as a scalable solution.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical piece of experimental hardware required for advanced AMO research, providing a robust, low-cost tool for time-resolved quantum optics experiments.
